turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Hi, everyone. Can you hear me? I'm on the train, so tell me if I cut out.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: We can hear you, Camille. There's a bit of noise, but it's fine.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: Same here.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Good. Is Saskia joining?

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: I'm here, I'm here. Sorry, my previous meeting ran over.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: No worries, Saskia. So, this is the review of Tuesday night's payments outage. The usual rule applies: we're looking for what broke, not for someone to blame. Ngozi, do you want to run it?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Sure. Torsten Lindqvist was on call, so I'll let him tell the story first, and then we'll go through what we change. Torsten, go ahead.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Okay. So at about eleven forty on Tuesday night, payments started failing. Not all of them at first, maybe one in five. By midnight it was almost every payment. I got paged at ten past twelve, thirty minutes after it started, which is one of the problems. I found the cause around twelve twenty, rolled back, and payments were working again at twelve twenty-seven. So about forty-seven minutes in total.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: Forty-seven minutes on a Tuesday night. How many payments is that?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: About one thousand eight hundred failed attempts. Most people tried again later, but we think around three hundred never came back.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: And quite a few of them came to us instead.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: We'll get to support, Rohan, I promise. Torsten, what was the cause?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: A configuration change to how long we wait for Horizon to answer. It went from thirty seconds down to three. Horizon is usually fast, but at night they run their own maintenance and they slow down. So our requests timed out, we retried, the retries piled up, and the queue filled.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: Who made the change?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Dashiell made it, as part of the checkout work. But I want to be clear, Saskia, Dashiell followed the process. The change was reviewed and approved. The process just never asked anyone to check what Horizon does at night.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: That's fair. I wasn't trying to point at Dashiell.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I know. I just want it in the notes.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Torsten, why did the alert take thirty minutes?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Because we alert on the size of the queue, not on failed payments. The queue grew slowly at first, so it only crossed the line at ten past midnight. With an alert on the payment error rate, it would have fired within two or three minutes.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: Can I say something about that?

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Go ahead, Rohan.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: The first ticket reached support at eleven fifty-two. By midnight we had about forty. The night shift had no idea what was going on, so for twenty minutes they told customers to try another card. Which obviously didn't help. Nobody from engineering told us anything until Torsten posted in the incident channel at twelve fifteen.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: To be fair, Rohan, I didn't know either until I was paged.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: I know, Torsten, I'm not blaming you. I'm saying our customers knew before we did, and that's embarrassing.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: It is. No argument there.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: And Brightwater Analytics noticed. Their finance team called our account manager at eight the next morning.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: What did they say?

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: They want a written report by the end of next week. About sixty of their renewals failed overnight.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Okay. I'll write to Brightwater Analytics myself. Rohan, can you send me the list of their failed payments by tomorrow?

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: By tomorrow noon, yes, Camille.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Now the bigger question. Saskia, I know this won't be popular, but I'd like to freeze every change that touches payments for two weeks, until the new alert and a proper review rule are in place.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: Two weeks? The new checkout goes out next Thursday. Brightwater Analytics is one of the clients waiting for it.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I know. That's exactly the code that broke on Tuesday.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: The setting broke, Ngozi. Not the checkout. We've tested the checkout for a month.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: We tested the setting too. It passed every test we had.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: So what, we stop shipping every time something goes wrong?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Can I add something here?

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: Sorry, go ahead, Torsten.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: The checkout work also changes how we retry payments with Horizon. If that goes out before the alert exists, and something breaks at night again, we're back to finding out from Rohan's team. I'd honestly be fine with one week instead of two, but not zero.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: One week I can probably sell. Two weeks, I'd have to call every client who's waiting.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: One week, then, if the alert and the review rule are both in. If they're not, the freeze stays.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: That's fine with me.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Okay, then let's decide. The checkout launch moves by one week, to the Thursday after next, on the condition Ngozi just gave. Saskia Brouwer, can you tell the clients who are waiting?

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: Yes. I'll message them by Friday. Brightwater Analytics too, unless you'd rather do it, Camille?

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: I'll put it in my letter. One less email for them.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Now the actions. Torsten, the alert on the payment error rate.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I can have it live by Friday. I'll test it by making payments fail on purpose in staging.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Good. I'll write the review rule. Any change to a Horizon setting needs a second reviewer from the payments team, and a short note on what happens at night. I'll have it written up by Wednesday.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: And for support, I want one thing, Ngozi. When an incident is open, someone tells my team in the first ten minutes, even if it's just to say we know and we're on it.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Yes, absolutely.

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: I'll write a short message template, so whoever is on call can just paste it.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Thanks, Rohan. And Torsten, thank you for Tuesday night. Forty-seven minutes isn't great, but you found it fast once you were paged.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Thanks. I'd rather not do it again soon.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: Should someone talk to Dashiell? I don't want him hearing about this secondhand.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I'll talk to Dashiell Prewitt this afternoon. And I'll ask him to help with the review rule, actually. He knows that setting better than anyone now.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Good idea, Ngozi. Let me recap. Torsten, the alert on failed payments, live by Friday. Ngozi, the review rule for Horizon settings by Wednesday, and the talk with Dashiell today. Rohan Pillai, the list of Brightwater Analytics payments by tomorrow noon, and the support template. Saskia, the checkout moves by one week, and you tell the waiting clients by Friday. And I send the written report to Brightwater Analytics by the end of next week. Anything else?

turns.speaker: c
turns.text: No, that's everything.

turns.speaker: d
turns.text: All clear.

turns.speaker: me
turns.text: Okay. Thanks, everyone. Torsten, go get some sleep.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: That's the plan, Camille.
